extracts.context: You hear two flatmates talking about a problem with their landlord.

unit.style: a natural conversation between flatmates, slightly frustrated

turns.text: Did you get a reply from the landlord about the boiler?
Finally, yes. He says he'll send someone on Thursday, which would be grand if he hadn't said exactly the same thing two weeks ago.
Honestly. We've been boiling kettles to wash for a fortnight. I think we should put it in writing this time, an email, so there's a record of when we first told him.
That's fair. I've just been phoning him, and he always sounds so reasonable on the phone that I end up apologising for bothering him.
Exactly, that's his technique. And if nobody turns up on Thursday, I'm going to check what the tenancy agreement says about repairs. There must be some kind of time limit.
Fine by me. You're much better at that kind of thing than I am.

questions.stem: Why is Niall unhappy with the landlord's reply?

options.A: The landlord has made the same promise before.
options.B: Thursday is not a convenient day for him.
options.C: The landlord has refused to pay for the repair.

questions.explanation: The landlord promised to send someone on Thursday, but he had 'said exactly the same thing two weeks ago'.
questions.evidence: if he hadn't said exactly the same thing two weeks ago

questions.stem: What does Grace want to do next?

options.C: start looking for a new flat

questions.explanation: Grace wants to send an email so that there is a record. Phoning is what Niall has been doing, without success.
questions.evidence: I think we should put it in writing this time

extracts.context: You hear two friends talking about a film they have just seen.

unit.style: a lively conversation between friends leaving a cinema

turns.text: So, what did you think? Be honest.
Honestly? The first hour was brilliant. The way they filmed the city at night, all those long silent shots... I was completely gripped.

But the ending. After all that build-up, the whole mystery was explained in about two minutes by a character we'd barely seen before. It felt like the writers had painted themselves into a corner and couldn't think of a way out.
I didn't mind that, actually. I thought the point was that the answer didn't matter. It was really a film about loneliness, not about the crime.
Maybe. You always find a deeper meaning, though. Sometimes a bad ending is just a bad ending.
Fair enough. I still want to see it again, though, if only to look at those night shots of the city one more time.

questions.stem: What did Jess particularly like about the film?
questions.explanation: She loved the way the city was filmed at night, with long silent shots. She does not mention the acting or the music.
questions.evidence: The way they filmed the city at night

questions.stem: What does Ethan think about the ending?

options.A: It was the weakest part of the film.
options.B: It mattered less than the film's real subject.

questions.explanation: Ethan says the answer to the mystery didn't matter because the film was really about loneliness. Jess is the one who thinks the ending was weak.
questions.evidence: It was really a film about loneliness, not about the crime.

extracts.context: You hear a student talking to her tutor about her final-year project.

unit.style: a calm, friendly conversation in a university office

turns.text: Thanks for seeing me, Doctor Shaw. I wanted to ask about my project. I've collected far more data than I expected, and I'm not sure how to fit it all in.

That's a nice problem to have, Ava. But you're right to be concerned. The most common mistake I see in final-year projects is students trying to include everything they've found. It makes the argument very hard to follow.
So should I just leave some of it out? It feels like a waste, after all those interviews.
Think of it this way. Your job isn't to show how hard you've worked; it's to answer your research question. Anything that doesn't help with that can go in an appendix, or nowhere at all.
OK. That actually makes me feel a lot better.
Good. Send me a new outline by Friday and we'll go through it together.

options.A: She does not have enough data.
options.B: She has more material than she can use.
options.C: She has missed an important deadline.

questions.explanation: She has collected far more data than expected and does not know how to fit it all in.
questions.evidence: I've collected far more data than I expected

questions.stem: What advice does Doctor Shaw give Ava?

options.A: to include only what answers her research question

questions.explanation: Anything that doesn't help to answer the research question can go in an appendix or be left out.
questions.evidence: Anything that doesn't help with that can go in an appendix, or nowhere at all.
